newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Labour blowing hot and cold on EMU.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Labour blowing hot and cold on EMU.

text.p: A top opposition spokesman has warned of the obstacles in the path of a decision by a Labour government to take Britain into a European single currency.
The warning is the most sceptical assessment yet of the chances of a rapid entry into the single currency if Labour wins the general election now due in less than seven months.
Labour, ahead in polls, has portrayed itself as staunchly pro-European to help deepen the rifts over Europe dogging Prime Minister John Major's efforts to control his Conservative Party.

But it has so far steered clear of saying whether or not it would sign up for the currency, prompting Major to accuse Labour of planning to commit Britain to a highly risky venture before it is clear whether or not it will work.

In weekend interviews, Labour's foreign affairs spokesman, Robin Cook, stuck to the party line, saying all options remained open and would be considered on the basis of the economic conditions and the national interest once Labour was in power.
But he told the Financial Times in an interview: "Any intelligent person can see that the obstacles are formidable."

And in a BBC interview, Cook warned that until Labour was confident Britain could match other European countries, especially Germany, in investment, skills and output, "it could be very risky to give up the option in future of devaluing".
Senior Labour aides insist that Cook's forthright opinions do not contradict the party's official "wait-and-see" policy.

But the comments by Cook -- a highly experienced operator unlikely to have spoken without gauging the political fallout -- highlight the fact the Conservatives are not alone in having divisions over Europe at the highest level of the party.

Cook is concerned about the potential impact on jobs of a single currency, as well as the prospect of a new government getting bogged down in Europe and losing sight of the domestic issues crucial to its survival.

Economics spokesman Gordon Brown is arguing strongly that a quick entry into a single currency would be in Britain's interests and could deliver a fatal blow to a Conservative Party already wounded by a general election defeat.
Both Cook and Brown are battling to convince Labour leader Tony Blair who, aides insist, is still undecided.

Cook's remarks underline growing confidence among those in Labour opposed to rapid entry that the debate is shifting their way, aided by a fear that if Labour does join the currency and the project fails, it could destroy the new administration.

Cook even outlined the way Labour could square a decision to stay out of a single currency in 1999 with its promise to restore Britain to the heart of the European debate -- by blaming the outgoing Conservative administration.

"I think there would be a lot of understanding... if we said...: "Look, we think it's a good project, we would have liked to join. But unfortunately the Conservatives have missed so many years of opportunity it may not be possible for us."
"Many of the governments of Europe would respect that."
Cook made it clear that his reluctance to entering a single currency was only in the short term.

The threat of speculation against sterling and the risk to inward investment could make membership essential -- probably around 2002 when national currencies are expected to have been comprehensively replaced by the single European currency.
"I think you could manage those in the short term if you didn't sign up in the first wave, but I don't think you could manage them indefinitely," Cook said.
